claims.interpretation_notes: MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN: The status line of this brief says 'PARKED 2026-09-03 on framing check 3 REVISE. NOT frozen, and no panel may run on it', with one framing-check finding still standing. I cannot see that finding (it is in run-record.md, which I do not have), so I cannot say which claim it affects or how. Methodology round 1 assumes a frozen brief. Computing verdicts over a brief that its own editors parked for an unresolved framing finding is exactly the endorsement risk this halt exists to prevent. I raise this on the brief's own stated status. It is not a defect I found independently: on my own reading, the three operationalizations are answerable and every ladder can reach every band. I answer the claim as posed alongside the concern. Classification: I could not open the report PDF (it exceeds my tool's 10 MB limit) or the eScribe attachments (HTTP 403). The only Roads-row figure I found is a third-party transcription citing the report's Appendix B p37. It gives Roads at replacement value $10,484M, Good 70.8%, Fair 16.2%, Poor (D+F) 11.2% for 2025. The primary ladder puts p = 11.2% in the 10% to below 25% band, so Partially supported. The failing part is the generality: 'the roads' as a whole are not rated poor on this measure. The alternative cutoffs give the same result (7.5% to below 20% band: Partially supported). The result is close to the primary 10% boundary (1.2 points above it), so confidence is Low until the figure is checked against the primary. I did not verify the City's exact class name, its sub-classes, the per-sub-class shares, the split between D and F, or a length-based distribution. I did not construct any road category. Excluded classes (bridges, sidewalks, streetlights, transit/LRT, buildings, parks) could not be listed item by item from the report.

claims.proposition_evaluated: At least $50.0 million of the $100.0 million approved for capital profile CM-20-0330 (Active Transportation Implementation Acceleration - Approach 3) came from funding sources whose terms permitted road or alley renewal instead.
claims.interpretation_notes: MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN: the brief says it is parked on an unresolved framing-check-3 finding and that no panel may run on it (see the first claim). I answer it as posed alongside that. Classification: the only funding source I found recorded for CM-20-0330 is tax-supported debt. The City's Capital Financial Update to 2023-12-31 lists 'Tax-Supported Debt - 100,000' (thousands). No grant was identified: the April 2023 federal Active Transportation Fund release funds Jasper Avenue and four planning studies and does not mention the $100M programme. Under the brief's rule, tax-supported debt is general municipal capital funding and is eligible unless the record says otherwise. So E = $100.0M, U = 0, X = 0, which is Supported under both the $50.0M and $25.0M cutoffs. Qualification that lowers confidence: Debt Management Fiscal Policy C203D (current version; C203C is superseded) allows tax-supported debt for renewal only as 'major rehabilitation of existing assets as a short-term strategy to eliminate a significant infrastructure renewal backlog'. FCS02696 (June 2025) warns that debt for renewal outside that definition conflicts with the policy. So the debt could lawfully have gone to major road rehabilitation, which the City has debt-funded before (High Level Bridge rehabilitation, LRV replacement, Hawrelak Park), but not to routine road or alley renewal without council changing or departing from its own policy. Neighbourhood and alley renewal are ordinarily funded by the dedicated Neighbourhood Renewal levy, not debt. A reader holding that routine renewal is what 'road renewal' means could put these dollars in U. I judge the policy to permit road renewal of the major-rehabilitation kind, which keeps E = $100.0M.

claims.proposition_evaluated: $100 million divided by the City's own published whole-infrastructure renewal shortfall for 2023-2026 (S) is at least 0.25.
claims.interpretation_notes: MATERIAL FRAMING CONCERN: the brief says it is parked on an unresolved framing-check-3 finding and that no panel may run on it (see the first claim). I answer it as posed alongside that. S: FCS02696 (City Council, 2025-06-10) says the '2023 to 2026 renewal investment shortfall is approximately $1.52 billion'. The ideal is about $3.6 billion ('about $3.6 billion', City budget FAQ) and $2.06B is allocated to renewal within the $9.44B approved budget. The City's own term is 'renewal investment shortfall'. It covers the same four years as CM-20-0330, so B2 is met. r = 100 / 1,520 = 0.066. That is Partially supported under the primary cutoffs (0.05 to below 0.25) and the alternative cutoffs (0.03 to below 0.15). The failing part is 'serious share'. Cross-check using the adopted-budget framing (Spring 2024 SCBA: 'ideal renewal investment was identified as $3.5 billion'; funded at '54 per cent'): the implied gap is about $1.61B, which is my arithmetic, not a City figure, and gives r of about 0.062, the same band. I did not read the adopted budget's pp42-49 heading for the difference, so the City's wording there is unverified. Required alternative (roads-and-alleys shortfall for 2023-2026): none found. FCS02696 says Neighbourhood Renewal and bridges received their full ideal funding, and the rest of the renewal programme was funded at 30.7% of ideal. So neighbourhood road and alley renewal was not where the shortfall sat, but I found no roads-only shortfall figure. Different-period figures, not classified: the 2023-2032 Capital Investment Outlook gap of $4.7B (r of about 0.021) and the January 2026 10-year funding shortfall of $10B (r of about 0.010).
